3720:
A critic is a person who carefully studies, evaluates, and judges something — and then shares that judgment, usually in words. The key idea is that a critic does not just say "I liked it" or "I didn't like it." A critic explains why something is good or bad, using thought, knowledge, and reasoning.

Think of a critic as someone whose job — or strong habit — is to look at something closely, weigh its strengths and weaknesses, and deliver a verdict that others can learn from.
The Two Main Ways the Word Is Used

1. A Professional Critic

This is someone whose actual job is to evaluate works in a specific field and share opinions publicly — usually in newspapers, magazines, websites, or on television.

Some common types of professional critics:

  • A film critic watches movies and writes reviews telling audiences whether a film is worth watching and why.
  • A music critic listens to albums or concerts and judges the quality of the music, the performance, and the artistry.
  • A literary critic reads books and analyzes them — examining writing style, themes, characters, and meaning.
  • A food critic visits restaurants, tastes meals, and evaluates the quality of the food, service, and experience.
  • An art critic examines paintings, sculptures, and other artworks, and interprets their meaning, technique, and value.

What all these people share is that they are knowledgeable experts in their fields. A film critic has watched thousands of films. A food critic has an educated and trained sense of taste. Their opinions carry weight because of that expertise.

2. An Everyday Critic

In casual, everyday language, a critic can simply mean anyone who regularly finds fault with something or someone. You might hear someone say, "My boss is my biggest critic," meaning their boss frequently points out what they're doing wrong. In this sense, the word is used more loosely, without implying professional expertise.
What Makes Someone a Critic, Not Just an Opinion-Giver?

This is an important distinction. Everyone has opinions, but not everyone is a critic. Here's the difference:

  • A random person might say, "That movie was boring."
  • A critic says, "That movie was boring because the screenplay failed to develop the characters meaningfully, the pacing in the second act was too slow, and the dialogue felt unnatural — unlike the director's earlier work, which balanced tension and emotion far more effectively."

A critic supports their judgment with analysis and reasoning. They break something down into its parts, examine each part, and then form a conclusion. Their goal is not just to express a feeling, but to illuminate — to help others see and understand something more deeply.

This is one of the most common misunderstandings about this word. Many people assume a critic is someone who only finds problems and tears things apart. That is not accurate.

A critic can — and often does — praise something. A good critic is balanced. They recognize both what works and what doesn't. When a music critic reviews a brilliant album, they will celebrate its strengths just as confidently as they would point out weaknesses in a poor one.

However, it is true that in everyday conversation, calling someone "a critic" or "critical" often leans negative — suggesting they focus too much on flaws. So the tone of the word depends on the context in which it is used.

Why do critics exist? What is their role in society?

  • They act as guides — helping people decide what to read, watch, listen to, or eat.
  • They act as interpreters — explaining complex works of art so that others can understand and appreciate them better.
  • They act as standards-keepers — holding creators accountable for quality, pushing the arts and other fields to improve.
  • They contribute to public conversation — a thoughtful review of a book or film can spark important discussions about culture, society, and ideas.

There is a long-standing tension between critics and the people whose work they judge. Creators — writers, directors, chefs, musicians — sometimes feel that critics do not fully understand the difficulty of making something. Critics, on the other hand, argue that an outside, informed perspective is exactly what is needed for honest evaluation. Both sides have a point. This tension is part of what makes the role of the critic both fascinating and controversial.

A critic is a careful, knowledgeable evaluator who judges something — a film, a book, a meal, a performance, or even a person's actions — and explains that judgment clearly and thoughtfully. The word can refer to a formal professional or, more loosely, to anyone in the habit of pointing out faults. A true critic is neither purely positive nor purely negative — they are honest, informed, and always able to explain why they think what they think.
3721:
Before diving into each meaning, here's a simple thread that runs through all of them:

"Critical" always points to something that deserves serious, careful attention — either because it involves judgment, because it is vitally important, or because it is at a dangerous turning point.

Keep that in mind, and each meaning below will make perfect sense.
Meaning 1: Finding Fault or Expressing Disapproval

This is the most everyday meaning. When someone is critical of a person or thing, they are pointing out what is wrong, weak, or flawed about it.

Examples:

  • "The manager was very critical of my report." → The manager found many problems with it.
  • "She is always critical of the way I dress." → She always points out flaws in how I dress.
  • "The newspapers were critical of the government's decision." → The newspapers disapproved and said what was wrong with it.

Important nuance: Being critical in this sense doesn't have to be unfair or harsh. Sometimes pointing out flaws is helpful and necessary. But the word does lean toward finding what's wrong, not what's right. If someone says nothing but good things about you, they are being "positive" or "supportive" — not critical.

Watch the grammar: In this meaning, "critical" is almost always followed by "of" — critical of someone/something. That's a reliable signal.
Meaning 2: Extremely Important — So Important That Everything Depends on It

Here, "critical" means something is so essential that if it's missing or ignored, the whole situation could fall apart. Think of it as the difference between something being nice to have versus absolutely necessary.

Examples:

  • "It is critical that you back up your files." → You absolutely must do this. Skipping it could be disastrous.
  • "Clean water is critical for human survival." → Without it, survival is impossible.
  • "This meeting is critical to the success of our project." → This meeting will decide whether the project succeeds or fails.
  • "At this critical juncture, every decision matters." → At this hugely important moment, there is no room for careless choices.

Close synonyms in this sense: crucial, vital, essential, key, indispensable.

How it feels: There is a sense of weight and urgency. Something critical is not just important — it is make-or-break important.
Meaning 3: At a Dangerous or Unstable Point — A Crisis

This meaning is very close to Meaning 2, but it adds a layer of danger, urgency, and instability. When something is critical, it is right on the edge — if the situation isn't handled properly, things could go very wrong.

You'll encounter this meaning most often in medical and emergency contexts.

Examples:

  • "The patient is in critical condition." → The patient is extremely ill and may not survive. Every minute counts.
  • "The dam has reached a critical level." → The dam is at a dangerously high water level; it could break soon.
  • "The economy is in a critical state." → The economy is in serious trouble; collapse is possible if nothing is done.
  • "He was listed as critical after the accident." → He was severely injured and in serious danger.

The feel of this meaning: There is a tipping-point quality to it. Things could go either way — toward recovery or toward disaster. That's what makes it critical.
Meaning 4: Involving Careful, Analytical Thinking and Judgment

This is a more intellectual, neutral meaning. When "critical" is used in this sense, it means approaching something with a thoughtful, analytical mindset — questioning it, examining it deeply, looking at both its strengths and weaknesses, and forming a well-reasoned judgment rather than simply accepting things at face value.

Examples:

  • "You need strong critical thinking skills to succeed in university." → You need the ability to analyze ideas carefully, question assumptions, and form your own reasoned opinions — not just memorize or accept what you're told.
  • "She wrote a critical analysis of the poem." → She carefully examined the poem — its structure, meaning, strengths, and weaknesses — and formed a well-argued opinion about it.
  • "The film received widespread critical acclaim." → Professional reviewers and analysts who carefully evaluate films praised it very highly.
  • "Read this article with a critical eye." → Read it carefully and thoughtfully; don't just accept everything it says — evaluate it.

The most important nuance here: In this meaning, "critical" does NOT mean negative. A "critical review" is not necessarily a bad review. A "critical analysis" is not an attack. It simply means the review or analysis is careful, thorough, and well-reasoned. In fact, critical acclaim — one of the most common phrases using this meaning — is entirely positive! It means experts who carefully evaluate things thought it was excellent.

This is a meaning that confuses many learners, so remember: analytical, not necessarily negative.
Meaning 5: Relating to a Specific Threshold or Tipping Point (Technical/Scientific Contexts)

In science and technical fields, "critical" refers to a precise point, level, or condition at which something changes fundamentally — below that point, nothing happens; at or beyond it, everything changes.

Examples:

  • "Critical mass" → In nuclear physics, this is the exact minimum amount of radioactive material needed to start a self-sustaining chain reaction. In everyday language, people borrow this phrase to mean the minimum amount of something needed to make a process work: "We need to reach a critical mass of users before the app becomes profitable."
  • "Critical temperature" → The specific temperature at which a substance undergoes a major change in its properties.
  • "The situation reached a critical point." → Things built up to the exact moment where a major change became inevitable.

The feel: There is a before-and-after quality. Below the critical threshold, one thing. At or past it, something entirely different happens.
How to Instantly Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Context is everything. Here are reliable patterns to look for:

  • "Critical of [person/thing]" → Finding fault (Meaning 1)
  • "Critical that / critical for / critical to" → Extremely important (Meaning 2)
  • "Critical condition / critical state / critically ill" → Dangerous, at a crisis point (Meaning 3)
  • "Critical thinking / critical analysis / critical eye / critical acclaim" → Analytical and evaluative (Meaning 4)
  • "Critical mass / critical temperature / critical threshold" → Scientific/technical tipping point (Meaning 5)

critically ill — so seriously sick that life is at risk.
"She was rushed to hospital and is critically ill."

critical acclaim — very high praise from careful, expert reviewers.
"The novel received critical acclaim but did not sell many copies." (The experts loved it; the general public didn't buy it in large numbers.)

critical thinking — the ability to analyze information carefully, question assumptions, spot weaknesses in arguments, and form reasoned conclusions.
"Schools should teach critical thinking, not just memorization."

self-critical — finding fault with yourself; being hard on yourself.
"She is too self-critical — she never appreciates her own achievements."

mission-critical — absolutely essential for a project or mission to work.
"The software update is mission-critical and cannot be delayed."

critical path — in project management, the sequence of essential steps that determines how long the entire project will take. Any delay on the critical path delays the whole project.

at a critical juncture / at a critical moment — at a hugely important and often difficult turning point.
"The peace talks are at a critical juncture."
The Single Thread That Ties Everything Together

Even though "critical" has five different meanings, they are all connected by one underlying idea:

Something critical commands your fullest attention — either because it requires judgment, because everything depends on it, because it is dangerously close to a breaking point, or because it marks the exact moment where things change.

Whether you are being critical of someone's work (you're judging it), a patient is in critical condition (a breaking point), a decision is critical (everything depends on it), or you are thinking critically (judging ideas carefully) — in every case, something serious, important, and attention-demanding is happening.

That's the soul of the word.
3722: "Criticism" means the act of examining something carefully and expressing a judgment about it — whether it is good, bad, or somewhere in between. However, the word has two distinct layers of meaning depending on the situation, and knowing both is what makes you truly understand this word.

In daily conversation, most people use "criticism" to mean pointing out what is wrong, flawed, or imperfect about something or someone. This is the sense you will encounter most often in life.

If your teacher says your essay lacks a clear argument, if your friend says your cooking is too salty, or if a manager says your presentation was unclear — those are all acts of criticism. The common thread is this: someone has identified a fault and expressed it.

"She struggled to accept criticism from her manager." Here, the manager pointed out her mistakes, and she found it difficult to hear.

"The politician faced severe criticism after the scandal." Here, many people publicly condemned the politician's actions.

"He is too self-critical." Here, the person judges himself too harshly, dwelling on his own flaws.

Notice that in all these cases, criticism refers to negative evaluation — something is being found wrong.

Not all negative feedback is the same, and this distinction matters enormously.

Constructive criticism is negative feedback given with the genuine intention of helping someone improve. It identifies the problem clearly and often suggests how to fix it. A good coach, teacher, or mentor gives constructive criticism — it may sting, but it is valuable because it points you toward growth. "Your introduction is weak because it doesn't tell the reader what to expect — try opening with your main point instead" is constructive criticism.

Destructive criticism, on the other hand, tears something down without offering any useful path forward. It focuses on attacking rather than improving. "Your writing is awful" with nothing more is destructive. It serves no constructive purpose and often feels like a personal attack rather than honest feedback.

Understanding this difference helps you both give and receive criticism wisely.
The academic and professional meaning: analysis and evaluation

In more formal settings — literature, film, art, music, philosophy, and science — "criticism" takes on a broader and more neutral meaning. Here, it refers to the careful, disciplined study and evaluation of a work or idea. Crucially, this kind of criticism does not mean only finding faults. It means examining something deeply and forming a thoughtful judgment, which can be positive, negative, or mixed.

Literary criticism is the academic study of books — analyzing a novel's themes, characters, structure, language, and historical meaning. A literary critic might conclude that a novel is a profound masterpiece. That conclusion is still criticism, because it is the result of deep analysis and judgment.

Film criticism is a professional reviewer's detailed assessment of a movie — its direction, performances, storytelling, and artistic value. Music criticism evaluates performances and recordings. Art criticism examines visual works. In each case, the "critic" (the person doing this work) is not simply complaining — they are analyzing and evaluating with expertise.

So when someone says "He is a respected film critic," it means he is a person who watches films carefully, thinks about them deeply, and expresses informed judgments about them. His review might be glowing praise — and it is still called criticism.
Criticism as a broader practice or discipline

"Criticism" can also refer to the overall practice or tradition of analysis and evaluation, not just a single act of it.

"Literary criticism has evolved significantly over the past century" means the entire field of analyzing literature has changed over time. "Social criticism is central to her writing" means she consistently analyzes and challenges the flaws or injustices she sees in society. In these uses, criticism refers to a body of thought, a discipline, or a sustained practice — not just one comment or review.
The difference between criticism and critique

These words are close relatives and are often used interchangeably, but there is a fine distinction worth knowing. A "critique" usually refers to a single, specific, and structured evaluation of one particular work or idea — and it tends to feel more balanced, formal, and thorough than general criticism. You might write a "critique" of a particular research paper, covering both its strengths and its weaknesses in an organized way.

"Criticism," by contrast, is the broader word. It covers everything: the everyday act of finding fault, the academic discipline of analysis, and the general practice of evaluating things. Think of "critique" as a specific, careful document or evaluation, and "criticism" as the wider concept that includes all forms of judgment and analysis.

The single most important thing to understand is this: "criticism" always involves judgment, but it does not always mean negativity. In daily life, it usually does mean pointing out flaws. In professional and academic life, it means rigorous analysis and evaluation — which may lead to praise, condemnation, or something in between.

The word can describe a single moment ("she gave him criticism"), a person's output ("his film criticism is widely read"), or an entire discipline ("literary criticism"). The common thread running through every use is this: someone is looking at something closely, thinking about it seriously, and expressing a considered judgment about it.
3723:
To criticize means to look at something — a person's behavior, a piece of work, an idea, a decision, or anything really — and point out what is wrong, weak, or flawed about it. You are making a negative judgment and expressing it.

If your friend writes an essay and you tell him, "Your introduction is confusing and your argument is weak," you are criticizing his essay. You are not just saying you dislike it — you are specifically identifying what is wrong.
The Two Sides of This Word

This is one of the most important things to understand about "criticize": it has two distinct meanings, and which one applies depends on the context.

Meaning 1 — The everyday meaning (pointing out faults):
This is how most people use the word in daily life. When someone criticizes you or something you did, they are expressing disapproval. They are saying, "This is wrong," or "This is not good enough," or "You made a mistake."

  • The teacher criticized the student for not completing the assignment.
  • People criticized the government's decision to raise taxes.
  • She criticized her brother for being irresponsible.

In this sense, criticizing has a negative tone. Nobody likes being criticized, because it feels like an attack on something you did or made.

Meaning 2 — The formal/academic meaning (careful analysis and judgment):
In fields like literature, art, film, and philosophy, "criticize" means to carefully examine something and give a reasoned, balanced judgment. This kind of criticism is not purely negative — it can point out both strengths and weaknesses. A professional film critic "criticizes" movies, but that doesn't mean they only say bad things; they analyze, evaluate, and give their informed opinion.

  • The scholar criticized the novel, highlighting both its brilliant use of language and its weak character development.
  • The architect's design was criticized for its innovation as much as its impracticality.

In this sense, criticizing is a thoughtful intellectual exercise. It requires knowledge, careful observation, and fair reasoning.

In everyday life, you will mostly encounter Meaning 1. Meaning 2 shows up more in academic writing, reviews, and professional discussions.
What Makes Criticism Different from Similar Things

Criticizing vs. Insulting:
When you criticize, you are talking about a specific thing — a behavior, a piece of work, an idea, a decision. When you insult someone, you are attacking who they are as a person. "Your report is poorly organized" is criticism. "You are a terrible person" is an insult. Criticism targets the thing; an insult targets the person.

Criticizing vs. Complaining:
When you complain, you are expressing your own displeasure about something — it's about how you feel. When you criticize, you are making a judgment about the thing itself — you are saying it has a flaw. "I hate traffic" is a complaint. "The city's road planning is inefficient" is criticism.

Criticizing vs. Condemning:
To condemn is stronger and more final. It often carries a moral weight — you are declaring that something is deeply wrong or unacceptable, not just imperfect. To criticize leaves more room for nuance and improvement. "I condemn this act of violence" is much stronger than "I criticize the way this was handled."

Not all criticism is the same in purpose or effect.

Constructive criticism is criticism that is meant to help. It points out what is wrong, but it also helps the person understand why it's wrong and often suggests how to improve. A good teacher, mentor, or coach usually gives constructive criticism. It is honest, specific, and respectful.

  • "Your presentation was hard to follow because you jumped between topics. Try organizing your points in a logical order next time."

Destructive criticism is criticism that tears something down without offering any path forward. It is often harsh, vague, or personal, and its effect is to discourage or hurt rather than to improve.

  • "Your presentation was a complete disaster. You clearly have no idea what you're doing."

Both are technically "criticizing," but their intent and impact are very different.
Who or What Can Be Criticized

Almost anything can be criticized:

  • A person's actions or decisions — "He criticized her for arriving late."
  • A piece of work — writing, art, music, films, architecture
  • Ideas, theories, or arguments — "Scientists criticized the flawed research."
  • Policies or systems — "Activists criticized the new law."
  • Yourself — You can criticize your own behavior or work. This is called self-criticism.

One important thing: criticizing someone's action is not the same as criticizing the person. Good criticism stays focused on what was done, not who the person is.

Criticism can range from mild to very sharp:

  • Mild: You gently point out a small flaw. "I think this paragraph could be a little clearer."
  • Moderate: You clearly state what's wrong. "This plan has several serious problems."
  • Harsh/Sharp: You strongly express that something is very bad. "This policy is completely irresponsible and dangerous."

The degree depends on how serious the flaw is and how strongly the person feels about it.

Criticism can be fair or unfair.

Fair criticism is based on real evidence, clear reasoning, and honest observation. It is proportionate — meaning the strength of the criticism matches the actual size of the problem.

Unfair criticism is based on personal bias, dislike, or emotions rather than genuine flaws. It may exaggerate problems, ignore the good things entirely, or attack things that aren't actually wrong.

When someone says "stop being so critical," they often mean: you are finding faults that aren't really there, or you are being harsher than the situation deserves.

• Fault (as in "find fault with"): Very similar to criticize, but often implies nitpicking small things.
  • Censure: Formal, official criticism — often used when an organization or authority formally disapproves of something.
  • Denounce: Publicly and strongly declare something is wrong, often in a loud or forceful way.
  • Reproach: To express disappointment or disapproval to someone, often in a sad or hurt tone rather than an angry one.
  • Nitpick: To criticize very minor, unimportant details — usually used negatively, implying the criticism is petty.
To praise, commend, compliment, approve of, or applaud something is the opposite of criticizing it. These words express that something is good or well done.

To criticize is to examine something and point out its faults or shortcomings. In everyday life, it means expressing disapproval of something specific. In formal or academic settings, it means to carefully analyze and evaluate something, giving a reasoned judgment. Criticism can be constructive (helpful and improvement-oriented) or destructive (harsh and discouraging). It can be fair or unfair. It is different from insulting (which attacks a person) and from complaining (which expresses personal feelings). At its best, criticism is honest, specific, and aimed at truth or improvement.
3724:
A critique is a careful, detailed examination of something — where you look at it closely, analyze how it works, identify what is strong about it, and point out what is weak, flawed, or could be better. It is not a simple reaction ("I liked it" or "I hated it"). It is a thoughtful, reasoned analysis that explains the why behind every judgment it makes.

Think of it this way: if you watch a film and say "that was boring," that is not a critique. But if you say "the film's pacing was slow in the second half because the director spent too long on subplots that didn't connect to the main story, which caused the emotional tension to drop right before the climax" — that is a critique.

A proper critique typically does all of the following:

1. Examines the subject closely.
It does not skim the surface. It digs into the details — the choices made, the structure, the logic, the evidence, the execution.

2. Makes judgments — but backs them up.
A critique doesn't just say something is good or bad. It explains why, with specific reasons and examples. This is what separates a critique from a mere opinion.

3. Covers both strengths and weaknesses.
A genuine critique is balanced. It acknowledges what works and what doesn't. If something is only praised with no flaws mentioned, or only attacked with no merits acknowledged, it is likely not a true critique — it is closer to flattery or complaint.

4. Is analytical, not emotional.
A critique comes from careful thought, not from gut reaction or personal feeling alone. The person giving the critique steps back, thinks carefully, and explains their reasoning in an organized way.

This is one of the most important things to understand. A critique is not the same as an attack.

A critique is serious, but it is respectful. In fact, when someone takes the time to write or deliver a real critique of your work, it means they are engaging with it seriously — they consider it worth examining. A shallow dismissal ("this is terrible") is the opposite of a critique.

The goal of a critique is to understand and often to improve. Even when a critique is harsh, its purpose is constructive — it exists to shed light, to reveal problems clearly so they can be addressed, or simply to help others understand something more deeply.

This is where many learners get confused, so let's clear it up:

Critique vs. Criticism
In everyday speech, "criticism" often sounds purely negative — it sounds like someone is finding fault and complaining. "Critique," on the other hand, carries the idea of balance and depth. You can give a critique of something you love as much as something you dislike. That said, in academic and professional contexts (especially in literature or philosophy), "criticism" is often used in the same neutral, analytical sense as "critique" — for example, "literary criticism" means the scholarly study and analysis of literature, not just finding fault with it.

Critique vs. Review
A review (like a film review or book review) is usually shorter, more impressionistic, and aimed at helping people decide whether to engage with something. A critique goes much deeper. It is more concerned with analyzing the craft, the structure, and the underlying logic than with simply recommending or not recommending.

Critique vs. Feedback
Feedback is more informal and conversational — your friend telling you what they thought of your essay draft, for instance. A critique is more formal, thorough, and structured. A critique is what a professor writes at the end of your paper; feedback is what a classmate tells you over coffee.

"Critique" appears in many fields:

  • Art and design: After students complete their artwork, the class holds a "critique" (often called a "crit") where everyone analyzes each other's work together.
  • Literature and film: Scholars write critiques of novels, films, and poems — examining how they are constructed and what they mean.
  • Academic writing: A professor might write a critique of a research paper, evaluating its argument, methodology, and evidence.
  • Music: A music critic writes critiques of albums or performances.
  • Philosophy and social theory: Thinkers write critiques of ideas, systems, or institutions — for example, a critique of capitalism or a critique of a philosophical argument.
  • Business: A manager might offer a critique of a business strategy, identifying its assumptions, risks, and blind spots.
A Simple Example to Lock It In

Imagine a student submits a short story. Here are three different responses:

  • Simple opinion: "I didn't enjoy it."
  • Criticism (in the negative sense): "The characters are weak and the ending makes no sense."
  • Critique: "The story has a genuinely original premise and the opening scene creates strong atmosphere. However, the main character lacks a clear motivation, which makes it hard to care about what happens to her. The ending feels abrupt — not because it is ambiguous (ambiguity can work), but because the story hasn't planted enough earlier moments for the reader to feel the weight of the final scene. With some restructuring of the middle section to develop the character's inner conflict, this story could be quite powerful."

Notice what the critique does: it is specific, it explains its reasoning, it acknowledges strengths, and it points toward improvement. That is what a critique is.
The Most Important Thing to Remember

A critique is engagement, not attack. It is what happens when someone takes something seriously enough to examine it with full attention and honest judgment. Whether the subject is a painting, a policy, an essay, or an idea — a critique treats it with enough respect to ask: "What is this trying to do, how well does it do it, and why?"
3725: A croak is a low, rough, harsh sound — the kind that feels like it comes from deep in the throat and has a scratchy, raspy quality to it. It is never smooth or musical. Think of it as the opposite of a clear, clean sound.
The Classic Example: Frogs and Toads

The single most well-known use of croak as a noun is the sound a frog or toad makes. When a frog opens its mouth and calls out, that short, deep, guttural sound is called a croak. It is not a chirp, not a whistle, not a squeal — it is something rougher and lower. If you have ever been near a pond at night and heard frogs calling, those repetitive, throaty sounds — that is what a croak is.

This is so central to the word that many people simply define croak as "a frog sound." That is not wrong, but the word is richer than that.
The Broader Picture: Any Sound With That Quality

The word croak is used for any sound — from any source — that shares that same rough, low, scratchy quality. The frog just happens to be the most famous producer of it.

Ravens and crows also produce a croak. Their call is not sweet or melodic; it is a deep, harsh, grating sound — a croak.

A human voice can produce a croak too. When a person has a very bad cold, a sore throat, has been crying for a long time, or has just woken up, their voice can lose its normal smooth quality and become rough and hoarse. When they try to speak or call out in that state, what comes out is a croak — or they speak in a croak. For example: "Help," she managed, but it came out as barely a croak. This means her voice was so damaged or strained that the word sounded rough, weak, and scratchy rather than clear.

To truly understand the word, here are the defining characteristics of a croak:

It is low in pitch. A croak is never high or squeaky. It sits low, in the bass end of sound.

It is rough and raspy. There is a scratchiness to it, like something is catching or rubbing inside the throat as the sound is made. It is never smooth or pure.

It is short and abrupt. A croak is not a long, sustained note. It is a short burst of sound — almost like a grunt, but with that distinctive rough texture.

It sounds strained or effortful. A croak gives the impression that producing the sound is not easy — that something is constricted or hoarse.

A croak can refer to a single sound ("A lone croak broke the silence of the swamp") or it can be used to describe the general type of sound something makes ("The croak of a raven echoed across the cliff"). Both uses are common and correct.
How to Use It in a Sentence

Here are natural examples that show the word working in real contexts:

  • The croak of frogs filled the warm summer night.
  • He tried to answer the phone, but all that came out was a croak — his voice was completely gone.
  • From somewhere in the dark, the croak of a crow made her stop walking.
  • "I'm fine," she said, though the words came out as a croak.
  • The old man's voice had turned into a tired croak after hours of speaking.

When croak is used to describe a human voice, it almost always carries a sense of weakness, illness, exhaustion, or emotional distress. A person speaks in a croak when their voice is not functioning at its best — when it is broken down in some way. This gives the word a slightly sad or vulnerable feel when applied to people. It is never used to describe a strong, healthy, confident voice.

A croak is a short, low, rough, and raspy sound — most famously made by frogs and toads — but also used for the calls of certain birds like ravens, and for the strained, hoarse sounds a human voice makes when it is sick, tired, or worn out.
3726:
Crochet is a handcraft that creates fabric or decorative objects by interlocking loops of yarn (or thread) using a single hooked needle.

The word "crochet" as a noun has two closely related meanings that build on each other:

1. The craft or technique itself
This is the skill, the activity, the art form. When someone says "She learned crochet as a child" or "Crochet is her favorite hobby," they are talking about the technique of making things by looping yarn with a hook.

2. The fabric or object produced by this technique
This is the physical result — the actual item or textile made through that process. When someone says "This blanket is made of crochet" or "Look at this beautiful crochet," they are referring to the finished work itself.

Both meanings come from the same source, and the context usually makes it clear which one is meant.

To truly understand the word, it helps to understand the process.

You take a length of yarn and a crochet hook — a small stick with a curved hook at one end, similar in shape to a tiny fishing hook. You use that hook to pull the yarn through itself, creating a chain of interlocked loops, one at a time. Each loop passes through the loop before it, and the loops lock into each other, building up into a stable fabric.

This process of pulling a new loop through an existing loop is called a stitch. You build rows or rounds of stitches, and as you add more, the fabric grows. The finished result is a mesh of interlocked loops — flexible, slightly stretchy, and textured.

Crochet fabric has a recognizable appearance. It looks like a series of small interlocked "V" shapes or loops arranged in neat rows. The texture is typically thicker and more raised than woven fabric (like the cloth in a shirt), and it often has a visible, slightly bumpy surface. Think of the texture of a chunky handmade blanket or a cozy winter beanie — that bumpy, looped texture is very often crochet.

The appearance can vary widely depending on the type of stitch used. Some crochet looks dense and solid (like a thick scarf or stuffed toy), while other crochet looks open and lacy (like a delicate shawl or tablecloth doily).
What can be made through crochet

One of the most remarkable things about crochet is how versatile it is. Among the things commonly made:

  • Clothing: sweaters, cardigans, hats, beanies, scarves, socks, mittens, gloves, tops, baby clothes
  • Home items: blankets, afghans (large decorative throws), pillow covers, dishcloths, pot holders, rugs
  • Accessories: handbags, tote bags, headbands, belts
  • Decorative objects: doilies (flat, circular lace-like pieces placed under vases or cups), wall hangings, flowers
  • Toys: stuffed animals and small figurines made through a Japanese-influenced style of crochet called amigurumi

The material can also vary. While yarn is the most common choice, crochet can also be done with fine cotton thread (for lace-like results), twine or rope (for bags and baskets), or even thin wire (for jewelry).

The tool that defines crochet as a noun — and distinguishes it from other crafts — is the crochet hook. It is a slim, pen-sized stick with a hooked tip at one end. It comes in many sizes; a smaller hook is used with thin thread for fine, delicate work, while a larger hook is used with thick yarn for chunky, warm items. The hook is what makes the technique possible — it grabs the yarn and pulls it through the loop, stitch by stitch.

People often confuse crochet with knitting because both involve yarn and create similar-looking fabric. But they are distinct crafts.

Knitting uses two long, straight needles (or circular needles) and keeps many stitches active on the needles at the same time. The stitches are smaller, more uniform, and the resulting fabric tends to be stretchy and smooth — think of the tight, flat weave of a classic sock or a pullover sweater.

Crochet uses one single hook and works only one active stitch at a time. The stitches are generally taller and the fabric tends to be thicker, denser, and more textured. Crochet is also generally considered easier to learn as a beginner. If you drop a stitch in knitting, the whole row can unravel. In crochet, that is far less likely because each stitch locks more firmly into the one before it.

A useful way to remember the difference: knitting = two needles, many active stitches; crochet = one hook, one active stitch.
How the noun is used in everyday language

Here are the different ways you will encounter "crochet" used as a noun in real life:

  • "She's been doing crochet for ten years." → referring to the craft/activity
  • "This is a piece of crochet she made herself." → referring to the object made
  • "The blanket is crochet, not knitting." → identifying the technique used to make an object
  • "He knows nothing about crochet." → referring to the subject or skill area
  • "That shop sells handmade crochet." → referring to crochet items collectively
The core idea to hold onto

If you had to summarize crochet in one sentence: Crochet is the craft of making fabric or objects by looping yarn together with a single hooked needle, and the word also refers to the items made this way. Everything else — the hook, the stitches, the blankets, the toys, the lace — flows from that central idea.

A crock-pot is an electric kitchen appliance used to cook food slowly, using low heat, over a long period of time — typically anywhere from 4 to 10 hours. It sits on your counter, plugs into a wall outlet, and does all the cooking on its own without you having to watch it.

Think of it as a self-contained, hands-free cooking pot.

A crock-pot has three parts:

An outer shell — usually made of metal — which houses the electric heating element. This is the part that plugs into the wall and generates heat.

An inner pot — this sits inside the outer shell and is where your food actually goes. It is most commonly made of ceramic or stoneware (a thick, heavy, clay-based material). This inner pot is sometimes called a "crock," which is where the name "crock-pot" comes from.

A lid — usually made of glass, so you can peek at the food without lifting it. Keeping the lid on is important because the trapped steam is part of what cooks the food.

A crock-pot works by surrounding your food with gentle, steady, low-level heat from all sides for many hours. It never gets blazing hot. Instead, it sits at a low, controlled temperature and slowly breaks down the food over time.

Most crock-pots have just two or three settings: Low, High, and sometimes Keep Warm. "Low" might cook your food in 8 hours; "High" might do the same job in 4–5 hours. That's it — there's no stirring, flipping, or watching required.

This method of cooking is called slow cooking.

Crock-pots are especially popular for:

Tough cuts of meat (like beef chuck, pork shoulder, or chicken thighs) — the long, slow heat breaks down the tough fibers and makes the meat incredibly tender, something quick cooking can't achieve as well.

Soups, stews, and chili — all the flavors slowly meld together over hours.

Beans and lentils, which need long cooking to become soft.

Casseroles and braised dishes.

Basically, anything that benefits from being cooked low and slow, in its own juices.

The biggest appeal is convenience. You put raw ingredients into the crock-pot in the morning, set it to "Low," go to work, and come home 8 hours later to a fully cooked, hot meal. The appliance does all the work unsupervised.

It's also great for flavor — long, slow cooking develops deep, rich tastes that fast cooking methods simply can't replicate. And it's economical, because it uses far less electricity than a full-sized oven running for hours.

This is an important distinction. "Crock-Pot" (with a capital C and capital P) is actually a brand name — a specific product originally created by a company. It's like how "Kleenex" is a brand name for facial tissue, or "Band-Aid" is a brand name for adhesive bandages.

However, over time, "crock-pot" (lowercase) entered everyday English as a generic term for any slow cooker, regardless of the brand. So when someone says "I made chili in the crock-pot," they almost certainly just mean a slow cooker — not necessarily the Crock-Pot brand specifically. Both uses are extremely common, and in casual conversation, "crock-pot" and "slow cooker" are used completely interchangeably.
A crock-pot is an electric countertop appliance with a ceramic inner pot that cooks food slowly over many hours using gentle, low heat — requiring almost no attention from the cook.
3728: Crockery is a collective word for the cups, plates, bowls, saucers, mugs, and similar items that you use when eating or drinking. These items are typically made from baked clay — such as earthenware, stoneware, porcelain, or china. Think of everything you'd lay on a dining table for a meal, excluding the metal utensils (spoons, forks, knives) and the glass items (glasses, tumblers). That group of things — the ceramic dishes — is what crockery refers to.
What it includes and what it does not

Crockery includes:

  • Dinner plates, side plates, dessert plates
  • Bowls (soup bowls, cereal bowls, serving bowls)
  • Cups, mugs, teacups, saucers
  • Teapots, jugs, gravy boats
  • Casserole dishes and baking dishes (when made of ceramic)

Crockery does not include:

  • Cutlery — the knives, forks, and spoons (those are metal)
  • Glassware — glasses, tumblers, wine glasses (those are glass)
  • Cookware — metal pots and pans used on a stove

This distinction is important. If someone asks you to "set the table with crockery," they mean put out the plates and cups — not the glasses or the spoons.

Crockery is an uncountable noun, which means it has no plural form. You cannot say "a crockery" or "two crockeries." Instead, you use it as a mass — a collective whole.

Correct: "The crockery is in the cabinet."
Incorrect: "A crockery," "two crockeries"

If you want to refer to individual items, you specify them: "a piece of crockery," or simply name the item directly ("a plate," "a bowl").
Where and how the word is used

Crockery is used when you're speaking about these items as a group, rather than naming each item separately. It's convenient when the specific item doesn't matter, or when you're referring to a full set.

Some natural examples:

  • "We need to wash all the crockery after the party."
  • "She packed the crockery carefully so it wouldn't break during the move."
  • "The kitchen shelf is stacked with crockery."
  • "The shop sells beautiful hand-painted crockery."

Crockery is a perfectly everyday, neutral word — not too formal, not too casual. You'd hear it in ordinary conversation, in shops, in households, in restaurants. It is more commonly used in British English. In American English, people tend to say "dishes" or "dinnerware" for the same thing, though "crockery" is understood in American English too.

Because crockery is made of baked clay, it is breakable. This fragility is a quietly understood part of the word's meaning. When someone says "be careful with the crockery," the warning about breaking is already built into it. You'd never say "be careful with the crockery" about plastic plates — even though plastic plates do the same job, they aren't crockery.

• Crockery set / dinner set — a matching collection of crockery (plates, bowls, cups, etc.) designed to look uniform
  • Fine china — a higher-quality, more delicate type of crockery, often kept for special occasions
  • Earthenware / stoneware / porcelain — these are types of materials that crockery can be made from (earthenware is the most basic and rustic; porcelain is the finest and most delicate)
  • Tableware — a broader word that covers crockery plus cutlery plus glassware — essentially everything used at the table
If you want to remember just one thing: crockery = the ceramic plates, bowls, and cups used for eating and drinking.
3729: A croissant is a type of baked pastry — a light, flaky, crescent-shaped bread made primarily from dough that has been layered with a generous amount of butter. It is one of the most recognizable pastries in the world.

A croissant has a distinctive curved, crescent shape — like a wide letter "C" or the shape of a quarter moon. Its outer surface is smooth and golden-brown, often with a slight sheen from being brushed with egg before baking. When you look at a croissant from the side, you can see thin, flaky, paper-like layers stacked on top of each other. This layered structure is one of its defining visual features.
What it's made of and how it feels

A croissant is made from a special kind of dough called laminated dough — which simply means dough that has been folded over and over with cold butter in between, creating dozens of thin, alternating layers of dough and fat. When this is baked in a hot oven, the butter melts and creates steam, which pushes those layers apart, giving the croissant its signature light, airy, and flaky texture.

When you pick one up, it feels surprisingly light for its size. When you bite into it:

  • The outside is crisp and shatters slightly, like thin, toasted pastry.
  • The inside is soft, airy, and slightly chewy, with a rich buttery taste.
  • It can be a little messy — flakes and crumbs often fall off as you eat it.

The flavour is rich, buttery, and mildly savoury with a very faint hint of sweetness. It does not taste sweet like a cake; it is more of a delicately flavoured bread with deep buttery richness.
Where it comes from and how it's used

The croissant is deeply associated with French culture, and is one of the most iconic items at a French bakery (called a boulangerie). However, it is now eaten all over the world, served at cafés, bakeries, hotels, and breakfast spots everywhere.

A croissant is most commonly eaten as a breakfast food or a light snack. It is typically eaten in one of these ways:

  • Plain, on its own, sometimes still warm from the oven
  • With butter and jam spread inside
  • With coffee — especially a café au lait or espresso — which is the classic French pairing
  • Sliced open and filled, like a sandwich, with ingredients such as ham and cheese, eggs, or smoked salmon
  • Dipped into a hot drink

While the classic croissant is plain and savoury-buttery, many variations exist:

  • Chocolate croissant (pain au chocolat) — a similarly made pastry but folded into a rectangular shape with pieces of chocolate inside. This is technically a separate but closely related pastry.
  • Almond croissant — a croissant filled or topped with almond cream and sliced almonds, often made from day-old croissants rebaked with this filling.
  • Cheese or ham croissant — filled with savoury ingredients, sometimes baked in.
  • Mini croissants — smaller versions, often served at buffets or as snacks.

In recent years, creative bakers have also invented hybrid pastries like the cronut (croissant + doughnut) and the cruffin (croissant + muffin), which use croissant-style dough in new shapes.
How the word is used in sentences

The word "croissant" functions as a straightforward countable noun:

  • "She ordered a croissant and a black coffee."
  • "The croissants at that bakery are made fresh every morning."
  • "He ate two croissants for breakfast."
  • "Would you like a plain croissant or an almond one?"

It can also be used as a modifier before other nouns:

  • "a croissant sandwich", "croissant dough", "croissant dough recipe"

If you had to hold on to just one idea: a croissant is a rich, buttery, crescent-shaped pastry with a flaky, layered texture, most commonly eaten at breakfast. It is not a bread roll, not a cake, and not a biscuit — it sits in its own category as a laminated pastry, recognisable by its shape, its layers, and its deeply buttery character.
